title: Abigail (1 Samuel 25)
hook: a wise woman rides out with bread and figs and talks David out of revenge

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cave, and your line was I will not lift my hand. Did a chance to get even come along, and did you let it go? Day seven hundred nineteen.

Yesterday David spared a king. Today he nearly kills a farmer over a rude reply. The farmer is Nabal, a rich man with three thousand sheep, shearing them in Carmel. David's men have been out in the fields with Nabal's shepherds and kept them safe, and now David sends ten young men to ask, politely, for whatever Nabal can spare for a feast day. Nabal sneers. Who is David? There are plenty of runaway servants these days. Why should I give my bread to men I don't know? The messengers come back and report. David gives one order: every man, gird on your sword. About four hundred of them strap on swords and set out. Somebody needs to get in the way.

One of Nabal's servants runs to Nabal's wife, Abigail. The text calls her a woman of good understanding, and her husband churlish and evil in his doings. She doesn't argue with her husband. She doesn't wait. She loads donkeys: two hundred loaves, two bottles of wine, five sheep ready dressed, parched corn, a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs. She sends them ahead, and rides out after them, and she tells Nabal nothing. On a hillside path she meets David coming down with his army. She gets off her donkey and bows to the ground. Then she speaks. She takes the blame on herself. She says her husband is just like his name: "as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him." And then she says the thing David needs to hear: when you are king one day, don't let this be a stumbling block on your conscience, that you shed blood without cause, that you avenged yourself with your own hand. She isn't only saving her household. She's saving David from himself. And David hears it. In the King James Bible: "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me: And blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand." Notice who he blesses. God, for sending her. Her advice. And her. In the cave, David held himself back. Here, someone else had to hold him back, and he was humble enough to let her. Later in the chapter Nabal dies, and David asks Abigail to be his wife.

Here's the practice: get ready to talk someone out of a rash act. Settle, and breathe. Is anyone near you riding down a hillside right now, with their sword on? A friend about to send an angry message. A family member about to quit, or storm off, or say the thing that can't be unsaid. Picture them. Then think the way Abigail did. Not how to win the argument, but what would help them see their better self. What could you bring? Bread first, words second. If you pray, you can ask for her kind of wisdom in your own words. If not, just picture the meeting on the path. The bell holds the time.
Abigail. Nabal's wise wife, who rode out with bread and figs and turned David back from shedding blood.
Your line: blessed be your wisdom. Today, if someone stops you from a rash act, thank them out loud, the way David did. Day seven hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Some Christians tell Abigail's story as an example of courageous peacemaking and wise speech, and it is read in Bible studies about anger, conflict and the gift of a wise friend.

fork.setup: you're Abigail. your husband has insulted David, and about four hundred armed men are on their way. what do you do?
options: load bread, wine and figs, and ride out to meet him.
fork.reveal: she loads the donkeys, rides out without telling Nabal, bows to the ground and talks David out of revenge. he blesses her advice.

original.note: Hebrew: Abigail, the wife of Nabal of Carmel in 1 Samuel 25.

trapdoor: what you thought: a side story about a picnic.
what it means: a wise woman rides into an army's path and stops a furious man from doing something he'd regret.
what a scholar hears: Abigail saves David from bloodguilt, and he blesses God for sending her, before he becomes king.

notes: Numbers are from the text: three thousand sheep (25:2), ten young men (25:5), about four hundred men (25:13), the provisions (25:18, which also lists five measures of parched corn).
The carry 'blessed be your wisdom' paraphrases 25:33, where the KJV has 'advice' (Hebrew ta'am, discernment). The script quotes the KJV and uses the index carry as given.
Nabal's death 'ten days' later (25:38) and David's marriage to Abigail (25:39–42) summarized; the script does not dwell on 'the LORD smote Nabal'. Confirm.
Original: name only; no etymology given.
Editor: 'the day before, in the cave' changed to 'in the cave' (1 Samuel 24 and 25 are not said to be a day apart); howItsDone 'Christians often' softened to 'some Christians'.
Audit: numbers and provisions checked against 1 Samuel 25:2, 5, 13, 18; quotations against KJV 25:25, 32-33. No change.
